title: Inhaled Corticosteroids in Asthma
subject: Medicine
summary: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of controller therapy for asthma, reducing airway inflammation and exacerbations. In low‑resource settings, selection depends on availability, cost, and local comorbidities. Clinicians must assess inhaler technique, adherence, and monitor for side effects.

sections.p: ICS are anti‑inflammatory agents delivered directly to the lungs. They are prescribed for persistent asthma when symptoms or exacerbations occur despite short‑acting bronchodilators.

Asthma severity is staged by symptom frequency, nighttime awakenings, rescue use, and lung function. The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) classifies into intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent.
In East Africa, common triggers include viral infections, indoor biomass smoke, dust, and parasitic infections. HIV and tuberculosis can worsen asthma control.
Patients with uncontrolled asthma present with wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, often worsening at night or early morning.
Spirometry is the gold standard but may be unavailable; peak flow monitoring and symptom diaries are useful alternatives.

t.b: Measures FEV1 and FVC to assess airflow limitation; a reversible drop >12% after bronchodilator indicates asthma
Provides daily baseline; a >20% variation suggests poor control
Elevated levels (>300/µL) predict better response to high‑dose ICS
Rule out pneumonia or pneumothorax if acute exacerbation

sections.p: ICS can mask infection signs and cause oral thrush, hoarseness, and, rarely, adrenal suppression.
b: Oral thrush – rinse mouth after inhalation
Adrenal suppression – avoid abrupt withdrawal in high doses

sections.p: Start low‑dose beclometasone or budesonide; titrate based on control. Use spacer to improve delivery. Reassess after 2–3 months.

t.b: Ask patient to demonstrate inhaler use; correct technique reduces failure
Tracks frequency of rescue use and nighttime symptoms; guides dose adjustment

sections.p: Educate on trigger avoidance, smoking cessation, and vaccination. Provide written asthma action plan.

t.b: Defines daily control level, rescue use, and when to seek urgent care

sections.p: COPD, viral bronchiolitis, and allergic rhinitis can mimic asthma but differ in age of onset, smoking history, and reversibility.
b: COPD – older age, smoking history, irreversible airflow limitation
Bronchiolitis – infants, viral prodrome, diffuse crackles
Allergic rhinitis – nasal symptoms, no nocturnal wheeze

sections.p: Spirometry may be normal in early asthma; peak flow can be affected by effort; eosinophil counts vary with infections.
b: Peak flow variability due to patient effort
Eosinophils low during acute viral infection

whenToSeekHelp: Severe wheeze unresponsive to reliever, cyanosis, stridor, or inability to speak in full sentences

faq.q: Why use a spacer with a metered‑dose inhaler?
faq.a: It reduces oropharyngeal deposition, lowers thrush risk, and improves lung delivery.

faq.q: Can I stop the inhaler abruptly if I feel better?
faq.a: No; sudden withdrawal can precipitate adrenal crisis and loss of control.

faq.q: What if spirometry is not available?
faq.a: Use peak flow monitoring and symptom diaries to guide therapy.

exam: 1. A 12‑year‑old boy with intermittent wheeze improves with albuterol. What is the next step? — Start low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid and assess inhaler technique. 2. A patient on high‑dose fluticasone develops hoarseness. What is the likely cause and management? — Oral thrush; advise mouth rinse and use spacer. 3.
